stories.headline: US approves $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

sources.body:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.

However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.

The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.

On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.

The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.

The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.

Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".

It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".

The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".

Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.

The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on.

In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".

He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.

Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.

It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
sources.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

sources.body:
The Ukrainian president called the US decision strong, but added that delivery of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠could take years

The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.

“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.

The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.

“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”

Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves ⁠of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.

On Thursday, a Russian drone ​strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform ‌in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five ‌died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.

Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.

He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.

Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington ⁠after US president Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.

One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring ‌forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, ​along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.

The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
sources.headline: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years

stories.headline: Rare US-brokered ceasefire enables civilian evacuation from Russian-occupied Oleshky

sources.body:
Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.

Ukrainian authorities confirmed the evacuees were on their way to southern Russia, from where they will travel on to Ukraine through Belarus.

Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".

Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".

A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.

"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."

Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.

They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.

Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.

Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.

The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.

But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.

Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.
sources.headline: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire

sources.body:
Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages

People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.

The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.

The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.

The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.

While Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.

Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.

“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.

Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.

While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.

Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.

Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”

Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.

Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.

“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”

Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.
sources.headline: Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky

sources.body: Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have left for Russia's Anapa city with a Ukrainian delegation, senior official David Arakhamia said Friday. They are expected to fly to Belarus before returning to Ukraine by bus, during a rare ceasefire brokered by the United States.
sources.headline: Residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in evacuation operation

stories.headline: Russia's Novaya Gazeta announces closure, citing escalating Kremlin pressure

sources.body:
At the editorial offices of Novaya Gazeta, they are packing up and shutting down.

Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.

For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.

Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.

It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.

"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."

"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.

"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."

In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".

The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.

Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.

The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.

As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.

In a statement on its website announcing the closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities.

"They've killed us," it starts. "The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."

The publication claims it is the victim of "a coordinated act" and blames "the repressive state apparatus".

"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime… The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.

Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the 'special military operation', new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
sources.headline: They strangled us, says founder of Russian newspaper shut under pressure from authorities

sources.body:
Independent outlet, whose former editor Dmitry Muratov won Nobel prize, cites intolerable pressure from authorities

Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent media outlets, has announced it will permanently close next month. The newspaper, whose former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 , cited intolerable pressure, including being stripped of its newsroom, its donation platforms and its legal right to publish.

“This is not just our own story; it is the story of a country and a society that are being systematically crushed,” wrote its editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, on the newspaper’s website.

Launched in the 1990s and for many years partly funded by the late Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya made its name through dogged, long-form reporting on corruption, rights abuses and social issues. Over the years, six of its journalists have been assassinated, including Anna Politkovskaya, who was gunned down in the stairwell of her Moscow apartment block in 2006.

While Novaya always swam against a tide of repression, the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made independent reporting almost impossible and decimated the Russian media landscape. Novaya was one of the last critical voices still operating from inside the country.

“For nearly five years of ***, we managed to keep working while being completely encircled by the security services. Now it’s over. We have found ourselves in a ‘kill zone’,” wrote Sokolov. The stars were used in place of the word “war”, as under Russian law, journalists must refer to the war in Ukraine as a “special military operation” or face consequences.

The newspaper’s first response to the invasion was to put out a special bilingual Russian-Ukrainian edition in the days after Vladimir Putin launched the invasion. It described the war as “madness” on its front page. Soon after, the Kremlin implemented draconian new censorship laws, which forced media outlets to publish only the Russian official narrative about the conflict.

“We said it’s not journalism and we’re not going to do that,” said Nadezhda Prusenkova, the head of Novaya’s press service. The newspaper published blank white spaces instead of euphemisms and false information, to provide a visible reminder of the censorship laws.

By the end of March 2022, Novaya decided to stop publishing its print edition altogether, but the threats and pressure only increased. In April that year, Muratov was doused with red paint while on a train , an attack that damaged his eyesight and that US officials say was carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence agencies. In September that year, the newspaper’s official licence was taken away and soon after their website was blocked in Russia.

Novaya’s journalists, long used to operating in a hostile environment, found ways to circumvent the bans. Many left Russia, and a number of exiled former employees set up Novaya Gazeta Europe , a legally distinct outlet. Muratov and a core team stayed behind and continued to publish a series of magazines with a print run of 999 copies, taking advantage of a law that means magazines with under 1,000 copies do not require an official licence. Novaya’s website continued running, too, although the Russian state hit the outlet with various new legal threats.
sources.headline: Russian society being ‘systematically crushed’ says Novaya Gazeta as newspaper announces closure

sources.body: Russia’s most renowned independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, announced on Friday that it was ceasing publication after more than three decades. Known for its courageous investigative journalism, the flagship newspaper said the Kremlin’s crackdown and ban on the media outlet had made it impossible to continue its work.
sources.headline: Russia’s Novaya Gazeta to cease publication amid Kremlin crackdown

stories.headline: Nearly 200 countries approve biodiversity agreements, though funding remains unresolved

sources.body:
In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries.

The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.

Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan.

"And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan.

Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature.

That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.

The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.

But according to the UN this week, the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets.

As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind.

"While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora.

"We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added.

This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."

But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".

Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection - an area bigger than Greenland.

Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.

Countries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money.

In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.

But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN.

At this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation.

Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment.

"A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."
sources.headline: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

sources.body: Almost 200 nations approved two agreements on Friday to halt biodiversity loss by 2030, following almost two weeks of negotiations that ran into extra time on the final day.
sources.headline: UN nature summit approves two key agreements after marathon negotiations

stories.headline: G20 family photo cancelled after countries refuse to appear alongside Russia

sources.body:
European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.

Two officials confirmed to BBC the cancellation of the "family photo" scheduled for Friday, which usually include representatives from all nations attending.

"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told his Russian counterpart at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Speaking with G20 foreign ministers on Friday, Miliband said that member countries must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine".

"Russia's war continues to cause colossal global harm - including the deaths of thousands of innocent civilians and disruption that hits energy and supplies and worsens food insecurity," he said.

"This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war."

Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.

One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".

"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.

The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
sources.headline: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister

sources.body:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott

The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.

Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.

“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”

About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.

European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.

During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.

A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.

“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”

The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.

Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.

That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.

“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
sources.headline: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia

stories.headline: Iran says four oil tankers are on fire in the Strait of Hormuz as Trump predicts the war will end soon

sources.body:
IRGC says four tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz, as Trump says war on Iran will ‘get wrapped up soon’.

Senators briefed on Trump’s ‘insane’ plan to restart war on Iran
sources.headline: Iran says four oil tankers on fire in Hormuz; Trump says war will end soon

sources.body:
As Washington and Tehran send mixed signals, analysts say trust remains a key obstacle to any deal.

Over the past week, Washington and Tehran have sent mixed signals about whether their eight-month war is heading back to full-scale strikes or towards a peace deal.

On Thursday, the head of United States Central Command (CENTCOM), Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on options for renewed attacks on Iran, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.

The US and Israel have drawn up joint plans to attack Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections, The New York Times (NYT) reported last week.

Yet on the same day, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance had offered to meet Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in person to negotiate an end to the war.

On Friday, Qatari mediators returned to Tehran for talks coordinated with the US, an official told Reuters.

So is Washington heading back to war, or towards a deal? Here’s what we know:

Essentially, Washington is preparing for war while keeping a diplomatic channel open.

The WSJ reported that the US has boosted air defences and munitions in the region and moved some troops away from bases vulnerable to Iranian retaliation.

Ten US military cargo planes landed at the Ovda and Nevatim air bases in Israel’s Negev region on Thursday, with more sent to Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, the Israeli public broadcaster Kan reported.

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, who said he had been briefed on the plans, called them “insane” and warned of a devastating escalation.

Vance’s letter, delivered to Rezaei through Qatari mediators on Sunday, proposed direct talks led by Vance, with Iran’s nuclear programme on the table from the start, according to the NYT, in a bid to prevent a renewal of strikes.

Whether it might have any influence over what happens next is a matter for debate. Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst who is an affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies in Sweden, described Vance as the “voice of reason” on Iran within the Trump administration, saying his signals have been “the least volatile and unpredictable”.

But he also told Al Jazeera that Vance’s position has “never proven to be sturdy enough to actually sway Trump”.

“Thus, while the optics with Vance look better than anyone else in the Trump administration, I doubt that they [Iranian officials] give the outreach much credence until Vance proves able to actually deliver something on his own,” he said.

Furthermore, Nader Hashemi, a professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera that “Rezaei is just one voice among many” adding that the “reality is that decisions are made collectively inside the Islamic republic”.

Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, has a different view, however, telling Al Jazeera, “There is no doubt that the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] currently calls the shots in Iran.”
sources.headline: US weighs new Iran strikes as Vance reaches out: Is war or a deal closer?

stories.headline: Republicans brace for potentially severe midterm losses, including in traditionally safe territory

sources.body: Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they’re set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife’s edge . House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they’ll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states. “It could be quite a brutal evening,” said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them.” Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump’s political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people. One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters. Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they’re facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day. Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who’d voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war. That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024. At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? “I think they’re bull,” he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump. Is he voting this time? “No,” Romero responded, adding: “I didn’t vote for this.” New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch. “Any Democrats telling you they aren’t winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations,” the senior Republican said. In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee “Vivek’s [Ramaswamy’s] numbers have gone off a cliff” in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton’s stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12. The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits. South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans’ base. “It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out,” said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party. But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South. Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes. “The cakewalk turned into a knife fight,” said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. “If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it’ll be a long night in Monroe,” the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago. In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump , and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson’s former pastor. Club for Growth poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff. "POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. “While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets,” said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they’ve long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster. Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas). The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed. Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden’s (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina’s open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they’re still not confident they’ll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It’s become the most expensive House race in history. The Republican in Kentucky’s 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people. Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races. Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district. “We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it,” Finstad said. “From a global perspective, people were like, ‘Well, you won by 18, you’re fine.’ And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it.” Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way. “I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what’s going to happen, they’re full of shit,” one senior Senate Democratic operative said. “Everything is close.” And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it’ll all soon be over. “I can see the light at the end of the tunnel,” said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. “It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it." Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report.
sources.headline: ‘It could be quite a brutal evening’: GOP braces for some once-unthinkable losses

stories.headline: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed asks former primary rival Haley Stevens to stay off the campaign trail

sources.body: TRAVERSE CITY, MICHIGAN — Michigan's Democratic coalition is fragmenting in real time days before a critical Senate election. After it seemed like former primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens might finally appear together, they’re back to sniping at each other. And it could hardly come at a worse moment as Democrats look to unite behind El-Sayed and hold on to a pivotal Senate seat. El-Sayed’s campaign is asking Stevens to stay away from all future campaign events in the closing days of the race, two people familiar with the decision, who were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive campaign dynamics, told POLITICO. She should stay away “as not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” one of the people said. The brushoff capped a day of the two lobbing increasingly pointed statements back and forth at each other, frustrating Democrats who say the infighting risks imperiling a state the party can hardly afford to lose as they try to flip control of the Senate. “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was squeezed out of the Democratic primary by the two other candidates, told CNN earlier on Friday, before El-Sayed issued his response. “People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.” Stevens did not immediately respond to a question on if she will now stay off the trail, and did not respond to an earlier question about whether her appearance was contingent on him apologizing. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment. El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens in a bitter and hard-fought primary in August that exposed division over support for Israel. The seat now held by the retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is crucial to Democratic hopes to take control of the Senate. Stevens and El Sayed have not campaigned together since a post-primary unity breakfast, but appeared on the verge of doing so earlier on Friday. Stevens initially said she would appear alongside El-Sayed and South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn at a church in Detroit on Sunday. But she said she expected the Democratic nominee to apologize for some of his past comments and condemn an ad run by an outside group supporting him that she described as antisemitic. The ad featured a conversation in a grocery store where a woman told a man they couldn't buy eggs because they had to set aside money for “killing Palestinians.” El-Sayed’s campaign had previously noted he was not affiliated with the ad. In response, El-Sayed did not touch on the ad or his past comments on Israel, instead saying that his campaign “has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing” and that that focus “is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70 [million] in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens.” “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. Privately, Democrats are frustrated — some with Stevens. “Every Democrat was singing the same tune but now, because one person is tone deaf, the whole choir is thrown off,” said a Michigan Democratic operative who is not directly working for El-Sayed’s campaign. Some Democrats tried to downplay the fight heading into the final days of the race. “There’s been a lot of efforts to coalesce Democrats, both from Abdul and from the congresswoman. I think everybody's on the same page of Democrats just beating Mike Rogers," said Joe Tate, a state representative from Detroit who supported Stevens in the primary and is now backing El-Sayed. But he acknowledged that "when you have people that have competed through a primary, I know it can always have those lingering effects." Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged Democrats to come together to support El-Sayed. “I've never met somebody who I agree with on 100 percent of everything,” Buttigieg told reporters while campaigning in the state for House candidate Callie Barr on Friday. “But when our health care is at stake, when a chance to have a more affordable everyday life is at stake, the choice is clear: Mike Rogers has disqualified himself.” Republicans have sought to play up the Democratic divisions. Rogers, in a Friday evening post on X , called Stevens a “courageous leader” and said she was “absolutely right” to call on El-Sayed to apologize. “I agree with her and my campaign is about being there, showing up and defending these communities and all Michiganders,” Rogers said. President Donald Trump, at a Friday night rally in Daytona, Florida, had a characteristically blunt message: "If you're Black, or if you're Jewish, and you vote for Abdul, you're not smart,” he said. Stevens’ comments so close to the pivotal election left some Democrats wondering what her goal was. “If you are someone with a large platform — whether you are, say, an outgoing member of Congress or an out-of-state streamer — who genuinely wants Abdul El-Sayed to become the next U.S. Senator from the state of Michigan and for Democrats to take back the Senate and put a meaningful check on Donald Trump, before you speak publicly I would implore you to ask yourself ‘is what I’m doing actually helping, or am I just seeking attention?’,” Democratic operative Adam Carlson, who has polled for a pro El-Sayed super PAC, wrote on X . Sophia Cai contributed to this report.
sources.headline: El-Sayed campaign wants Stevens to stay away after day of back-and-forth sniping

stories.headline: Democrats warn a favorable midterm environment could mask the party's unresolved weaknesses ahead of 2028

sources.body: Democrats are poised for a good night next Tuesday. That doesn’t mean they’ve figured out how to win. More than a dozen lawmakers, campaign operatives, strategists and pollsters warned in interviews that national Democrats risk drawing the wrong conclusions if they take back control of at least one chamber of Congress next week. Those figures from across the party worry that the midterms, which have become a referendum on President Donald Trump, have done little to improve the Democratic Party’s brand. They caution that a favorable political environment has papered over persistent problems for a party still grappling with why it lost the 2024 presidential election. And they admit they are still sharply divided over what its message should be heading into 2028. “Don't confuse them losing with us winning,” said Morgan Jackson, the senior adviser to Democrat Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign in North Carolina. Cooper has consistently led in the polls by a wide margin in a state Trump won three times. “This is not an affirmation of the Democratic Party in any which way,” said one veteran Democratic pollster working on Senate campaigns, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “It is very much a rejection of Trump.” The Democratic Party’s approval rating plummeted in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election, and remains relatively weak. That’s even as voters tell pollsters they are more likely to trust Democrats than Republicans on several fronts, including addressing the cost of living, which voters consistently say is their top issue this cycle. Democrats’ quest for a coherent, positive pitch to answer rising prices and perceived corruption in Washington has at times been stymied by infighting between the party’s progressive and moderate factions over the best way to respond to the Trump administration. Democrats fought over whether to prolong government shutdowns to protest funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the slashing of health care subsidies in late 2025 and early 2026. They were quick to attack their own upon release of the Democratic National Committee’s formal autopsy on where the party went wrong in 2024. But as Americans soured on Trump’s agenda and the Iran war drove up costs, Democrats zeroed in on a broad “costs, chaos and corruption” message that blamed the White House — without having to resolve their own internal tensions and disorder. “When your opponent is destroying themselves," said Matt Barron, a Democratic strategist who has done work across the rural Midwest and Rust Belt, "just get out of the way and let it happen.” Nabbing wins in a midterm election with a historically unpopular president is one thing. Building a winning brand for a party that was soundly defeated at the polls just two years ago is another. “If all you do is say the other people are terrible, that only gets you so far,” said Democratic donor Oliver Libby, who has advised Democratic House candidates Cait Conley in New York and Johnny Garcia in Texas this cycle. “You can have a minimum viable product of a midterm with criticism. You definitely don't win a presidential year with just criticism.” In a new POLITICO Poll conducted by PF Global, more than half of Americans said if Republicans lose control of both the House and the Senate, it would be either because of Trump’s actions since he became president, or because Republicans have run weak campaigns. Just one in four said a Democrat-controlled Congress would be because the party had run a strong campaign. “There are people who are going to vote in this election who are going to vote against Republicans,” said Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist and adviser to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. “That does not mean they are in love with Democrats. It just means they are voting against the people in charge.” Democratic strategist Lis Smith, an architect of Pete Buttigieg's 2020 presidential campaign, said the Democratic candidates performing well in historically deep-red territory are the ones distancing themselves from the national party. “That should tell party leaders something,” she said. Smith helped found the moderate groups Majority Democrats and The Bench, and is advising Democratic Senate candidates like Adam Hamilton in Kansas, James Talarico in Texas and Josh Turek in Iowa — all of whom have taken on that tack. In Kansas, Hamilton publicly asked former Vice President Kamala Harris to stay away from his campaign, and said he would vote against Chuck Schumer remaining the party’s leader in the Senate. In Texas, Talarico vowed to challenge the party’s “establishment” and “change the Democratic Party.” And in Iowa, Turek says he rarely thinks about the party, while Rob Sand, the Democratic gubernatorial candidate in the state, has said he wants to end the two-party system altogether. “The reality is that a lot of very average and even mediocre candidates get across the line in a wave election,” Smith said. “A wave can hide a lot of weaknesses, and so we need to be able to make sure that the party can survive when the wave recedes.” Assuming Democrats take back control of at least one chamber of Congress next week, top party operatives see an opportunity for their side to deliver for voters who have wanted more checks on the Trump administration’s expansive use of executive power. But many caution that Democrats on Capitol Hill should avoid leaning too hard into an anti-Trump message next year, while others argue that the anti-corruption message will continue to galvanize the electorate. "The thing that I would be concerned about, if you go from 2026 to 2028, is that people think that corruption, that elite control over our economy, is just a Trump issue," said Bill Neidhardt, who worked on Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign and is now advising left-leaning Democratic candidate Will Lawrence and working to boost Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan. “What they need to focus on is that corporate power, those billionaire elites who are dictating the terms of our economy, that's what people are upset with." William Garcia, the co-chair of Wisconsin’s La Crosse County Democratic Party, has been canvassing extensively for his party in the state’s rural-heavy 3rd district , where voters swung toward Trump in recent years . Democrats are now trying to claw back that support. “I think we’re going to have a great night on Nov. 3. And then all these Democrats are going to have to deliver on all of these things we’re talking about,” Garcia said. “If we get to the end of 2027 summer and we haven’t passed bills to make a substantial difference in people’s lives, that’s my biggest fear. We gotta deliver.” Others acknowledge that voters may hold the party to a higher bar if they succeed in taking back control of both chambers of Congress — and they’ll be ready to punish Democrats in 2028 if they don’t follow through on their campaign promises to hold the Trump administration to account and bring down the cost of living. It’s a slippery slope for a party that has historically struggled to convince voters that it is well equipped to handle the economy. In 2024, Trump persuaded the majority of voters they would be financially better off with him in the White House, while painting Democrats as a party more concerned with social issues. “If we start getting back into a party that cares more about non-economic issues, then we haven't learned the lesson,” warned Pete Giangreco, a veteran Democratic strategist who has worked on House, Senate and gubernatorial campaigns this cycle. “People just are going to keep hitting the change button until the economy starts working for them again.” Samuel Benson and Meredith Lee Hill contributed reporting.
sources.headline: 'A wave can hide a lot of weaknesses': Dems question if they'll learn anything

stories.headline: New polling finds that only one in four Americans trusts political polls to estimate election results accurately

sources.body: This just in, according to new poll results: Americans don’t trust polls. Only 25% of Americans said political surveys correctly estimate votes, according to a new POLITICO Poll , conducted by PF Global. The result reveals that a significant portion of the public lacks faith in the industry as it contends with accusations of consistently failing to reach Republican voters. It comes amid an intensely scrutinized 2026 midterm cycle, where public polling and campaigns’ internal polls have shown many races within the margin of error in key battlegrounds and in once-safe red territory. Roughly one in four respondents say that polls showing a blue wave coming in November are wrong, and they expect Republicans to win key races. And 41% of Americans — including voters of both parties — either say polls tend to underestimate Democrats or that they tend to underestimate Republicans. There have been some high-profile blunders: Polls have missed the mark throughout the Trump era. This cycle alone, surveys in Democratic primaries incorrectly predicted that progressive Francesca Hong would win the race for Wisconsin governor and that Abdul El-Sayed — who did become Democrat’s Michigan Senate nominee — would win by a much wider margin than the 1 percentage point victory he eked out. Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans have cast doubt on the latest forecasts: The polls are “grossly underestimating Republican enthusiasm around the country,” Johnson said on Fox News this week, adding that “more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys.” President Donald Trump has called the polls “fake” and “rigged.” Vice President JD Vance said he tells people to ignore the polls because they have a “demotivating effect on our voters.” Pollsters know their industry is facing heavy scrutiny. However: “There isn't another thing waiting in the wings to replace the full purpose of this tool,” said Charlotte Swasey, the director of analytics for the Democratic think tank Searchlight Institute, told POLITICO. “This is what we have, and it's difficult, it's increasingly difficult. But it's not dead by any sense of the word.” Pollsters have made a number of changes over the years — like capturing respondents across all levels of education attainment or adjusting their methodologies to account for low response rates among any given group.   Still, roughly two in five Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 say political polls tend to underestimate Republicans. Their feelings are not completely unfounded. In 2016, pollsters grossly underestimated support for then-candidate Trump, with most polls coalescing around a relatively secure victory for former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton. Distrust is especially widespread among Trump voters who identify as “MAGA Republicans” — his most loyal base. Three in five MAGA Trump voters say the polls indicating Democrats will win key races next week are incorrect. Among non-MAGA Trump voters, just a third feel the same. “National polls always underestimate support for Republicans,” said RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. “Polls may suggest one thing, but the American people get the final say, and Republicans remain laser-focused on driving voters to the polls, defying history, and protecting our majorities." “I do think that non-response among base Republican voters in some of these red states is a problem,” Christine Matthews, president of public opinion polling firm Bellwether Research, told POLITICO in a recent interview . Republican candidates and officials are banking on the non-response caveat as Senate races in states like Kansas, Mississippi and Nebraska — and to some extent, in South Carolina and Louisiana — all tighten, with less than one week until Election Day. If polling proves true, they could experience once-unthinkable losses in deep-red territory. But distrust is not limited to Republicans. Many in both parties were outraged after one group — Wedgewood Polls — admitted under scrutiny from FiftyPlusOne to using fake data in its polling results in several Democratic primaries, which some believe impacted election results . Another group published fake polling data on the Los Angeles mayoral race as a test to see how the data would travel before being verified. And just under a third of voters who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris say political polls tend to underestimate Democrats. Part of the distrust can come down to the fact that polls are not intended to forecast outcomes. They are a snapshot of public sentiment at a given point in time — and people can change their minds. One in five Americans said in POLITICO’s survey they have filled in a poll on how they would vote differently than how they actually voted. “Of course there are people who say something to a poll and then do something different a couple of weeks later,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at London-based PF Global, POLITICO’s polling partner. “I think it's quite possible that some of the races that were real big misses earlier this year were decided in the very last week.” According to a recent POLITICO survey, polls — which, when conducted correctly, involve careful planning and meticulous methodology — don’t earn much more trust than prediction markets, where odds are determined simply by bets placed by the public. Just 18% of people said they trusted poll-based forecasts over prediction markets to correctly predict the outcome of an election. That’s a marginal lead on the 12% of people who said they trust prediction markets over polls. A third said they trust neither. Still, most voters say they do make decisions based on polling. Roughly 55% of Americans say they would “definitely” go vote if the polls showed their preferred candidate far behind. Even among Republican midterm voters who say the polls underestimate their party, roughly 75% say the same. “There are a lot of voters that are motivated to send a message to the system,” said longtime GOP strategist Kevin Madden. “I think particularly on the [political] right, they'll be motivated to send a message, and essentially that message is ‘You're wrong, and the voters are right.’” The big question for campaigns is “are there enough of those?” he said.
sources.headline: Poll: Americans don’t trust polls

"></img><p>A las <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/un-error-humano-a-las-836-la-cadena-de-fallos-y-decisiones-con-las-que-el-gobierno-explica-la-nueva-tragedia-en-la-linea-madrid-sevilla.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/un-error-humano-a-las-836-la-cadena-de-fallos-y-decisiones-con-las-que-el-gobierno-explica-la-nueva-tragedia-en-la-linea-madrid-sevilla.html">8.31 del miércoles</a>, seis trenes que circulan por la línea de alta velocidad que une Madrid-Sevilla y se reparten por un tramo de 63 kilómetros se ven afectados por el mismo problema: se ha caído el sistema LZB, que sirve para que dos convoyes no coincidan en el mismo cantón o pequeño segmento de la línea. La consecuencia es inmediata. Todos se paran. Saben que van a tener que operar al amparo los sistemas ASFA (que mide la distancia entre trenes por balizas y es capaz de detenerlos si superan ciertas barreras de seguridad) y BSL (que se comunica con los trenes por señales en los laterales de la vía). Los maquinistas se ponen en contacto con el centro de coordinación de Adif en Atocha (Madrid), donde nadie parece sorprendido por la situación, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-28/el-controlador-de-atocha-al-maquinista-del-ave-desconecte-y-vuelva-a-conectar-y-reanude-con-marcha-normal.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-28/el-controlador-de-atocha-al-maquinista-del-ave-desconecte-y-vuelva-a-conectar-y-reanude-con-marcha-normal.html">según los audios publicados por EL PAÍS</a>. En lo que va de año, el LZB ha dejado de estar en servicio en 170 ocasiones, según explica luego el ministro Óscar Puente. El govern espanyol ha defensat el sistema de seguretat de l'alta velocitat dos dies després de l'accident entre dos trens d'alta velocitat a Toledo . El ministre de Transports, Óscar Puente , ha sortit a donar explicacions i, sense assenyalar cap treballador en concret, ha dit: "De moment sembla que hi ha hagut un error al centre de comandament d'Adif".

La investigació se centra en les ordres que el centre de control d'Atocha va donar al maquinista de l'AVE un cop havia caigut el sistema de seguretat automàtic, l'LZB.

Segons Puente, només aquest 2026, l'LZB ha fallat 170 vegades , una xifra que ha situat "dins la normalitat". Tot i la freqüència, quan aquest sistema cau, els trens passen a circular en mode manual.

Aquest mode, que consisteix en semàfors i indicacions des del centre de control, no incorpora un bloqueig automàtic que freni el tren quan es detecta un obstacle a la via, i no és prou potent per evitar possibles errors humans.

El ministre s'ha excusat dient que, "en el sistema ferroviari, l'aeri i el marítim, quan els sistemes fallen, és l'ésser humà qui entra a controlar l'entorn".

L'ésser humà és l'última ràtio en tots els casos, però no està sol amb un paper i un boli.

El secretari general del sindicat de maquinistes (Semaf), Diego Martín , ha criticat que, en aquesta situació, el control recaigui en les persones i no en una tecnologia robusta de seguretat:

Com més vegades la seguretat depengui de les persones, més gran és el risc.

Dimecres al matí, quan falla l'LZB i s'aturen tots els trens, el maquinista de l'AVE contacta amb el centre de control d'Atocha i avisa amb el codi Meta 000 , que vol dir que el tram de via fins a Urda està ocupat per un altre tren.

En aquesta situació, el reglament de circulació ferroviària indica que un cop restablert el sistema, el tren ha de reprendre la circulació amb " marxa a la vista ", és a dir, a una velocitat molt baixa que permeti aturar-se en cas de necessitat.

Però a les 8.36, amb l'LZB encara sense funcionar i amb l'Iryo aturat al davant, des del centre de control s'ordena que reprengui la marxa a velocitat normal .

Aquest és el primer error que es desprèn de les comunicacions parcials filtrades entre el centre de control i els maquinistes . El segon error és una confusió en la conversa entre el controlador i la maquinista de l'Iryo.

Des del centre de control, també es dona l'ordre a l'Iryo que torni a circular i el semàfor que té al davant es posa en verd.

A les 8.41, la maquinista avisa Atocha que no pot arrencar el tren : "He tingut una pèrdua de transmissió a velocitat Meta 40 . Estic aturada al senyal d'entrada d'Urda".

El codi Meta 40 vol dir, al contrari del Meta 000, que la via està lliure i el protocol marca que es pot reprendre la marxa. Tot i això, la maquinista alerta que està aturada.

Minuts més tard, a les 8.48, torna a avisar que no pot reiniciar el sistema: "Encara estic aturada".

Als àudios publicats se sent com el controlador diu: "El 6076 (Iryo) està amb un Meta 40 fins que s'aturi, està avançant fins que s'aturi ".
sources.headline: El debat de la seguretat a l'alta velocitat: de la caiguda de l'LZB a l'error al centre de control

Centro de control de la circulación de Adif en la Estación de Francia de Barcelona 

El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, compareció por segunda vez después de que el miércoles dos trenes, un AVE y un Iryo, colisionaran a la altura de Urda (Toledo) en la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla, provocando 69 fallecidos. ¿Qué ocurrió según el ministro que acabó provocando la tragedia?

El LZB es un sistema de señalización, protección y supervisión automática de trenes. Este sistema cae el pasado miércoles a las 8.31 horas en un tramo de 63 kilómetros de la línea Madrid-Sevilla. ¿Por qué cae? Puente reitera que es por un fallo de comunicación entre ordenadores.

A partir de ahí la gestión recae en el centro de Adif de regulación y control (CRC) de alta velocidad de Atocha y los trenes pasan a funcionar no solo con las indicaciones que reciben desde el CRC, sino con un sistema secundario de bloqueo ferroviario (BSL) y otro de protección automática del tren mediante balizas (ASFA). El LZB es más seguro y robusto. ¿Por qué? Porque gracias a él, un maquinista sabe en todo momento la posición del tren que le precede y del que le sigue y el sistema regula la velocidad para que haya suficiente espacio entre ellos por seguridad. Cada tren se encuentra en un tramo propio (llamado cantón), que en el caso del LZB es virtual, mientras que en los otros sistemas es físico y de mayor tamaño: de semáforo a semáforo.

Puente recordó que hay dos garantías que rigen la circulación ferroviaria. La primera: no puede haber dos trenes en un mismo cantón. La segunda: tras caer el LZB, se puede reanudar la marcha a la vista (a una velocidad máxima de 40 km/h) para que el maquinista pueda reaccionar y frenar el tren en caso de advertir algún peligro en la vía.

Desde el CRC se le dice a las 8.36 h al maquinista del AVE, después de la caída del LZB, que puede reanudar el trayecto amparado en el BSL y a marcha normal. Hay que recordar que el AVE acaba impactando contra el Iryo a más de 160 km/h.

A las 8.41 h el CRC autoriza a la maquinista del Iryo, parado frente al semáforo previo a Urda, a reanudar el trayecto en BSL. No obstante, el tren no puede arrancar. “No sé qué pudo pasar”, arguyó Puente, añadiendo que tendrá que ser la investigación y la jueza quienes lo determinen.

La maquinista del Iryo vuelve a contactar con el CRC minutos después de la primera llamada explicando que no puede reiniciar el LZB y que por eso todavía permanece parada frente al semáforo previo a Urda, aunque este ya está en verde. Sin embargo, Atocha no frena al AVE a pesar de que el Iryo acaba de informarles que permanece parado. Minutos después (8.53 h) se produce el impacto a más de 160 km/h.

El ministro asegura que en todo momento la gigantesca pantalla que ocupa gran parte de la sala del CRC en Atocha muestra la ubicación de los dos trenes y que los operarios podían verlos. Entonces, ¿por qué nadie frenó al AVE? “Habrá que investigarlo. Se ven dos trenes en el mismo cantón. Cuando el tren (AVE) reanuda la marcha se ve como va ocupando progresivamente uno y otro sector, pasando de verde a rojo, y como se aproxima al tren Iryo, que está detenido en el sector que está en rojo al final del cantón, y desgraciadamente pasa mucho tiempo sin que nadie le advierta de que hay un tren parado”.

Decisión pendiente.El ministro, ayer en rueda de prensa, explicó que el Ejecutivo estudia la posibilidad de que la línea de alta velocidad entre Barcelona y Madrid corte por obras 

El Gobierno se está planteando cortar por un plazo de entre uno y dos años la línea del AVE para acometer a pleno ritmo las obras de mejora que están previstas y que, de llevarse a cabo con el servicio en marcha, tardarían alrededor de cinco años. El ministro Óscar Puente ha anunciado la posibilidad de suspender la principal línea de alta velocidad en España , que mueve cerca de 40.000 pasajeros al día, durante la rueda de prensa sobre el accidente.

Puente ha respondido a una pregunta directa sobre detener la alta velocidad entre Barcelona y Madrid en un contexto en el que se tienen en cuenta varios factores además del de la fiabilidad de las reformas a medida que se vayan aplicando. La línea transportó el año pasado 14,4 millones de personas, con una caída del 1,7% respecto al 2024 que comenzó a partir del accidente de Adamuz. “Es ahora mismo una de las cosas que estamos valorando, pero no solo por una cuestión de seguridad, sino por múltiples razones”, ha indicado el ministro

La recuperación de la certeza en el funcionamiento del sistema de alta velocidad sería uno de los principales motivos para cerrar la línea mientras se reforma para reforzar la seguridad y se adapta a una velocidad máxima de 350 kilómetros por hora, frente a los 300 km/h que permiten los trenes y la infraestructura actual.

“La falta de confianza no solamente estriba en la seguridad, sino también en la fiabilidad y en la puntualidad”, ha observado Puente “El accidente —ha señalado— nos pone sobre la reflexión del conjunto de lo que estamos ofreciendo a los ciudadanos. Y creo que una forma de recuperar confianza no solo es la pata de la seguridad, sino también la de la fiabilidad y de la puntualidad”.

La principal comparación que ha establecido el ministro ha sido con el modelo alemán para hacer este tipo de mejoras de líneas ferroviarias. “En el sistema en el que se viene trabajando tradicionalmente en Alemania —ha apuntado—, en casi todas las ocasiones, cuando hay que afrontar una renovación de línea, se corta el servicio y se procede a renovar la línea de manera completa, derivando el servicio a los usuarios durante el tiempo en el que esas obras tienen lugar”.

En España no se ha aplicado nunca una restricción tan radical, desde la puesta en marcha de la primera línea del AVE, entre Madrid y Sevilla, que se inauguró en 1992. Precisamente en los próximos meses se terminarán las obras que se iniciaron en el 2022 en ese tramo y del que ya sólo queda pendiente la sustitución del sistema de seguridad LZB por el EMRTS que la homologará con el estándar europeo.

“Nuestro sistema es el opuesto —ha contrapuesto Puente—, en España se prima la prestación del servicio a la realización de las obras, con las consecuencias de que digamos que la fiabilidad, la puntualidad, la seguridad, yo creo que no, pero la fiabilidad y la puntualidad sin duda se ven afectadas”. “Es algo que nos estamos planteando, no lo oculto. Tenemos que tomar decisiones”, ha explicado.

Una mujer camina por el andén junto a un tren de AVE de Renfe estacionado en las vías de la Estación de Atocha. / JESÚS HELLÍN / EUROPA PRESS - Archivo

El Ministerio de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible valora cortar la línea de alta velocidad entre Madrid y Barcelona mientras se ejecutan las obras de remodelación que está previsto que empiecen en 2027 , según ha revelado el ministro Óscar Puente en su segunda rueda de prensa desde que se produjo el accidente en Urda (Toledo) el miércoles y en la que ha descartado que vaya a dimitir.

El ministro ha explicado que España suele mantener la prestación del servicio mientras se realizan obras de mejora de la infraestructura ferroviaria, a diferencia de países como Alemania, donde en casi siempre que hay que remodelar una línea se corta ese tramo y se priva a los usuarios de su uso durante el tiempo en el que las obras tengan lugar. La ventaja, en el caso alemán, es que las obras acaban antes.

Sin embargo, en España se suele mantener el servicio y las labores de remodelación se realizan en horas en las que no hay trenes circulando o se realizan cortes puntuales, de forma que la intervención se demora más en el tiempo. La principal desventaja de esta fórmula es, según el ministro, que en muchos casos se ve afectada la "puntualidad" y la "fiabilidad" de la ruta en cuestión.

"Si tomamos la decisión de seguir el ejemplo alemán habrá contestación (ciudadana), pero no sé si en estas circunstancias es la fórmula más prudente", ha reconocido Puente. En ese caso, el ministro ha dicho que el plazo de ejecución de las obras se podría reducir de cinco años a entre 12 y 24 meses . La línea Madrid-Barcelona fue la segunda en entrar en operación en España tras la que une la capital con Andalucía y la primera en dar entrada a la competencia a Renfe (Iryo y Ouigo). Esta es la línea de alta velocidad más utilizada de todo la red, con 3,3 millones de pasajeros en el último trimestre de 2025 , un tercio de los 10,6 millones de usuarios de la alta velocidad en España, según la Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC).

Puente ha aclarado que esa decisión no tiene que ver con reforzar la seguridad de la línea tras el accidente de Urda (Toledo) --ha aclarado que en ese tramo "no había obras en curso" que hubieran afectado al sistema de seguridad LZB o que hubieran podido tener que ver con el siniestro--, sino que si se está valorando "darle una vuelta al sistema" se debe a tratar de mejorar la reputación del sistema ferroviario tras el desprestigio al que se ha visto abocado en los últimos meses.

"No es por el accidente en sí, sino porque el accidente nos hace reflexionar sobre el servicio que ofrecemos al ciudadano y una de las cuestiones es la fiabilidad y la puntualidad del servicio prestado", ha añadido el ministro. Al accidente de esta semana en Urda (Toledo) y al ocurrido a principios de año en Adamuz (Córdoba) se suma el incremento de las demoras y las incidencias en la red ferroviaria española , que es cada vez más habitual desde que se liberalizó el tren en 2020 y se dio entrada a la competencia de Renfe.
